chapters.title: Chapter 7: Capstone: Building and Defending a Capacity-Aware Scaling Plan

lessons.title: Final Case Study: A Full Capacity Analysis for a Systematic Strategy

children.text: One last, fully worked case study, on a fresh strategy, walking every one of the eight framework steps from earlier in this chapter, start to finish. Nothing new to learn here, just everything from this course applied once, in order, to one real decision.
The Strategy: Quality-Momentum on Nifty Midcap 150
Buy Nifty Midcap 150 stocks in the top quintile of a combined quality and 6-month momentum score, rebalanced every two months, holding around 18 positions at a time.

Applying the square-root law and turnover-adjusted capacity formula from Chapter 4, with a 2% annual cost budget: AUM_max = 35 x (0.02 / (6 x 0.72 x 0.018))^2, which works out to roughly Rs 2.32 crore per stock.
With 18 concurrent positions, treated as independently capacity-constrained, total theoretical portfolio capacity comes to roughly Rs 41.7 crore.

Every position is capped at the smaller of Rs 2.32 crore, the liquidity-derived limit, or 6% of total AUM, a concentration limit set for this midcap book. At low AUM, concentration binds. As AUM grows, the fixed liquidity cap increasingly takes over.

body.label: Practical Operating Capacity
body.context: Applying a 65% safety margin to the Rs 41.7 Cr theoretical estimate, per Chapter 4

children.text: Track rolling IC monthly, correlation to published quality and momentum factor indices quarterly, and position overlap against any other strategy the desk runs, per Chapter 3's monitoring framework.
Step 7: If This Strategy Approaches Its Ceiling

Turnover here is already low, 6 times a year, so per Chapter 5's diagnostic principle, ADV is the more binding factor, not trading frequency. The right lever is extending the same methodology into a deeper-liquidity universe, such as a Nifty 50 sleeve, or adding a genuinely independent strategy, not trying to trade this exact book any faster.
Execute rebalances using POV capped near the per-stock liquidity limit, and benchmark every fill against VWAP and implementation shortfall, per Chapter 6.

body.title: Recompute at a Lower Turnover
body.prompt: If this strategy's turnover were reduced to 4 times per year instead of 6, holding ADV, sigma, Y, and the cost budget fixed, what would the new per-stock capacity be, in Rs Cr? Round to two decimals.
body.explanation: AUM_max = 35 x (0.02 / (4 x 0.72 x 0.018))^2 = 35 x (0.02 / 0.05184)^2 = 35 x 0.3858^2 = 35 x 0.1488 = Rs 5.21 Cr, more than double the 6x-turnover figure from a turnover reduction of only 33%, another reminder of how strongly capacity depends on turnover.

body.text: Every number in this case study came from ideas covered earlier in this course: ADV and the square-root law, the turnover penalty, position sizing discipline, a safety margin, ongoing monitoring, a correct scaling diagnosis, and disciplined execution. None of it is complicated on its own. What makes it work is doing all eight steps, in order, every time, instead of stopping at the first one that happens to look good.

points: A complete capacity analysis walks through all eight framework steps in order, from a raw per-stock estimate to a monitored, executable operating plan.

Correctly diagnosing whether a strategy's constraint is ADV-driven or turnover-driven determines which scaling lever will actually help, exactly as this strategy's low turnover pointed toward deeper liquidity rather than faster trading.
A modest reduction in turnover can meaningfully expand capacity, since the relationship is governed by the square of turnover, not a simple proportional one.

The skill this course has built is not any single formula, it is the habit of asking how much capital a strategy can actually hold, and revisiting that answer as conditions change, before finding out the hard way.
